products.tagline: The honest $150 start. No shame in starting here.
products.blurb: A 70mm refractor on a simple mount — the classic answer to 'what's a cheap first telescope?' for a decade. It won't beat an 8-inch Dob, obviously, but the Moon looks fantastic and there's zero learning curve. If the hobby doesn't stick, you're out the price of a nice dinner.

products.name: Nikon Aculon A211 10x50
products.tagline: The 10x50s you'll still own in twenty years.
products.blurb: Before a telescope, after a telescope — you always need 10x50s. The Aculon is the benchmark budget pair: bright, sharp enough, and tough enough to survive being lent to curious friends. Scan the Milky Way, split double stars, catch satellites. Instant, handheld, wonderful.
pros: Useful forever, even with a telescope

products.name: Telrad reflex finder
products.tagline: Point at the sky like pointing with your finger.
products.blurb: A reflex sight that projects glowing rings onto the sky — no magnification, just 'put the thing in the circle.' Star-hopping with a Telrad feels so natural you'll wonder why all finders aren't like this. The best $40 upgrade for any Dobsonian owner, and I don't say that lightly.
pros: No magnification — see the real sky
cons: Needs a dark site to shine

products.name: Large planisphere (40°N)
products.tagline: The whole sky on a spinning wheel. No charging cable.
products.blurb: Dial in tonight's date and time, and this shows you exactly what's overhead. No app, no phone glare wrecking your night vision, no dead battery at 11pm. Learn the sky on one of these before you let a computer do it for you — future you will be grateful.

products.name: Orion SkyQuest XT6
products.tagline: The 6-inch Dobsonian that raised a generation of stargazers.
products.blurb: A 150mm f/8 Dobsonian that's been the default first serious telescope for decades — because it works. Long focal length means crisp, contrasty Moon and planets. If you want one telescope that does everything well and never talks back, it's shaped exactly like this.

products.name: Celestron Cometron 7x50
products.tagline: Forty bucks. A thousand hobbies started right here.
products.blurb: 7x50 is the classic astronomy binocular format: bright, steady, wide. The Cometron is the cheapest honest pair — for the price of two pizzas you get the Milky Way, comets, and star clusters. Keep them by the back door; you'll reach for them more than you think.
pros: Bright 7x50 views, easy to hold steady

products.name: Celestron NexYZ 3-Axis Smartphone Adapter
products.tagline: Your phone + any telescope = photos tonight.
products.blurb: Clamps your phone to almost any eyepiece and nails the alignment — the fiddly part of phone astrophotography, solved for sixty bucks. It's the bridge between 'I saw it!' and 'look what I caught.' If you ever want to show someone what that light in the sky actually was, start here.
pros: Fits almost any phone and eyepiece

products.name: Red LED headlamp
products.tagline: Hands-free red light. Future you says thanks.
products.blurb: Red mode on, both hands free for eyepieces and focus knobs, night vision intact. After the red flashlight, this is the most-used twenty bucks in the kit. You'll wonder how you ever observed without one — probably while holding a flashlight in your teeth, like the rest of us did.

products.name: Canon EOS Rebel T7
products.tagline: The people's astrophotography DSLR.
products.blurb: 24 megapixels, a mountain of cheap used lenses, and it plays perfectly with the Star Adventurer 2i. Add a $100 nifty-fifty and a tracker, and you're shooting nebulae. Nothing fancy — just the honest, affordable way into the deep sky.
pros: Pairs perfectly with a star tracker
cons: Kit lens is limiting for deep sky

products.name: Celestron NexStar 6SE
products.tagline: The 8SE's lighter little brother. Easier to carry, still finds everything.
products.blurb: Same GoTo brain as the 8SE in a 6-inch package you can actually carry to a dark site without negotiating with your spine. You give up some light-gathering; you gain a scope that leaves the house more often. And the best telescope, as I keep saying, is the one you actually use.
pros: Much lighter than the 8SE — genuinely portable
Long f/10 focal length great for planets and the Moon
cons: Less light grasp than the 8SE for deep sky
Batteries drain fast in the cold

products.name: Vortex Diamondback HD 10x42
products.tagline: The 'buy once' binoculars.
products.blurb: Brighter, sharper, and tougher than budget pairs, with Vortex's lifetime warranty — they'll fix it even if the damage was your fault. (We've all dropped things in the dark.) For night-sky scanning plus daytime birding, this is the pair you stop upgrading from.
pros: Noticeably sharper and brighter than budget 10x42s
Lifetime VIP warranty — Vortex fixes or replaces it

products.name: Celestron Nature DX 8x42
products.tagline: Wider, steadier, friendlier — especially if 10x feels shaky.
products.blurb: An 8x42 with a wide field and forgiving eye relief: easier to hold steady, easier on the eyes, lovely for sweeping the Milky Way. If 10x50s make your hands feel like they've had three coffees, these are your pair. No shame in it — steady views beat shaky magnification every time.
pros: Wider field than 10x42s — easier to find things
Steadier hand-held views, forgiving eye relief
cons: A bit chunky for its class

products.name: Turn Left at Orion
products.tagline: The book that teaches you what's actually up there.
products.blurb: One object per spread, star-hop maps, and honest sketches of what each target looks like through a small scope — not Hubble photos that set you up for disappointment. Over 100,000 copies sold. If you buy one astronomy book, let it be this one. (This is me, your 表哥, insisting.)
pros: Shows exactly what objects look like in a small telescope
Star-hop instructions you can follow at the eyepiece
cons: Not a substitute for a real star atlas
Heavy book to juggle at the telescope

products.name: Sky & Telescope's Pocket Sky Atlas
products.tagline: 30,796 stars in your coat pocket. Never needs charging.
products.blurb: The most recommended star atlas in the hobby: 80 charts down to magnitude 7.6, compact enough to take anywhere. It'll never crash, never update at the worst moment, and works at every dark site on Earth. Pair it with a red flashlight and you're officially an observer.
pros: 80 charts with 30,796 stars — deep enough for a telescope
Pocket-size, dews up less than big atlases
The standard reference every observer recognizes
cons: Print is small — bring a red flashlight and readers
Pages stick together in heavy dew
Jumbo edition exists if the pocket print is too small

products.name: Cheshire collimating eyepiece
products.tagline: Ten calm minutes with this beats guessing forever.
products.blurb: A sight tube with a crosshair that takes the mystery out of collimating your reflector. New Dobsonian owners fear this job far more than they should — with a Cheshire it's a peaceful ten-minute ritual, and your views will thank you for it.
pros: One purchase serves every reflector you'll own
cons: Learning curve the first couple of times
Won't fix a fundamentally bad mirror

products.name: Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 STM
products.tagline: The nifty fifty: f/1.8 of pure night-sky value.

products.name: ZWO Seestar S50
products.tagline: Point it at the sky. Watch galaxies appear on your phone.
products.blurb: A 50mm smart scope that finds, tracks, and stacks everything by itself — you just watch deep-sky objects materialize on your screen. No eyepiece, no learning curve, no frozen fingers. Purists will grumble; you'll be too busy showing your friends the Whirlpool Galaxy to care.
pros: Fully automated — plate solving finds targets itself
Live stacking shows deep-sky objects from light-polluted skies
cons: Needs a charged battery and your phone/tablet
Screen observing isn't the same as eyepiece observing
